paper_read.note: 41-page paper: 5-page covering report, then five appendices (A Treasury Policy, B Strategy, C Investment Criteria, D Prudential Indicators, E Liability Benchmark). Went to Finance, Policy and Resources Committee on 12 February 2026; this document (500019888) is the Council re-presentation for 3 March 2026 (both dates now past). Read in full from local disk. Officer address published on page 5 of covering report (Fenella Merry — Executive Director of Finance for both Richmond AND Wandsworth via the Better Service Partnership joint treasury team; email domain @richmondandwandsworth.gov.uk reflects that). Loan-book reconciliation DOES NOT TIE — our file at 2025-12-31 shows 12 PWLB loans / £45.4m against the paper's £92.4m PWLB (part of £107.9m total including MEEF £10.5m and Barclays £5m); recorded in facts, kept out of the email per PIPELINE guidance. Balance-sheet identity also doesn't close cleanly against the paper's own stated internal borrowing (£60.7m implied by arithmetic vs £82m stated in para 4.18). Draft is written from Appendix D section C (financing costs ratio doubling), Section 3.2 / Appendix B section 8 / Appendix D section B (MRP methodology change and its numerical footprint), Appendix D section J (interest-rate-risk sign inversion in 2026/27), and Appendix E (£45m 2026/27 borrowing calculation).

Serves as EDF for both Richmond AND Wandsworth via the Better Service Partnership (main-report para 4.11: 'Treasury Management for both Councils is undertaken by a single team').

Not on the recipient line.

facts.value: £107.9m at 31.12.25, all fixed rate, average interest rate 3.1%. Composition: £92.4m PWLB, £10.5m MEEF (Mayor of London's Energy Efficiency Fund), £5.0m Money Market (single Barclays loan). Para 4.25 rounds to '£108m of external borrowing'.

source.title: Appendix B — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, page 2 (External Borrowing table); main report para 4.25 (page 6)

facts.note: Since 2014 new loans have been taken out on an annuity basis (Appendix B page 3). No new external borrowing taken in 2025/26 (para 4.17). Long-term external borrowing 'is anticipated to be taken in 2027/28' (Appendix B page 4 — the summary bullets), though the paper also carries a plan of £145m over the next four years (para 4.17) and £22.9m of external borrowing in the Change-in-CFR table for 2026/27 (Appendix D B page 30).

source.title: Appendix D section B — Capital Financing Requirement, page 30

facts.note: The 2028/29 step is driven by £67.7m of new external borrowing planned for that year alongside £54.8m change in CFR. IFRS 16 lease additions of £17,294k already sit in the 2024/25 opening CFR figure. The Change-in-CFR line takes £5,801k → £9,021k of MRP off the total across the horizon.

facts.value: Paper's own statement: 'accumulated internal borrowing of £82m as at 31st March 2025' (para 4.18). Arithmetic implied from CFR £198.6m less Projected External Debt £137.8m gives £60.7m — a £21m gap.

source.title: Main report para 4.18 (p.5); Appendix D section B (p.30); Appendix D section F (p.31)

facts.note: Projected External Debt of £137.8m explicitly 'includes both direct borrowing and indirect borrowing implied in a financing lease or PFI arrangement' (Appendix D F). Treasury loans at Dec 2025 were £107.9m per Appendix B page 2, implying c.£30m of OLTL (leases + PFI) embedded in the £137.8m. The paper's £82m internal-borrowing figure may sit on a different definition or approximate boundary. Kept OUT of the email — a treasurer knows their own working and doesn't need the arithmetic pointed out.

facts.value: DOES NOT CLOSE CLEANLY. 31.3.25: CFR 198,576 − Projected External Debt (incl leases) 137,829 = 60,747 arithmetic implied internal borrowing. Paper's stated internal borrowing 82,000 (para 4.18). Gap ~£21m.

source.title: OUR arithmetic — paper Appendix D B (p.30) and F (p.31) vs main report para 4.18 (p.5)

facts.value: DOES NOT TIE. Our file at 2025-12-31 (borrower 'RICHMOND UPON THAMES LONDON BOROUGH C'): 12 PWLB loans, principal £45,431,084, weighted 3.4263%. Paper Appendix B page 2 at 31.12.25: PWLB £92.4m. Gap ~£47m of PWLB principal missing on our side.

source.title: OUR file — price_book.py 'RICHMOND UPON THAMES LONDON BOROUGH C' --as-at 2025-12-31; paper Appendix B page 2

facts.note: As-at 2026-08-16 our file shows 22 live PWLB loans totalling £88,333,413 — so the file has gained ~10 loans / ~£43m between Dec 25 and Aug 26. Paper's para 4.17 says 'The Council has not taken any external borrowing so far this financial year and current monitoring suggests no external borrowing will be needed in 2025/26' — so the 10 new loans in our file must be 2026/27 drawdowns (April 2026 onwards). Even after those additions, our Aug 26 total (£88.3m) still sits below the paper's Dec 25 PWLB figure (£92.4m) — the file appears to be missing pre-2025 loan history for this borrower name. Data-quality issue on OUR side, not evidence of anything in Richmond's paper. KEPT OUT OF THE EMAIL per PIPELINE guidance; briefly disclosed as a coverage gap without invitation to correct us.

facts.value: Methodology change: 'Previously this was calculated on a straight line basis for an average of 33 years, with a maximum of 50 years... It is proposed that the calculation for MRP should now consider the life of the asset it is financing (unless this is not known).' Appendix B section 8 (p.12) markup shows strikethrough on '50 years' and insertion of 'the life of the asset or where that is not known 50 years will be used as a proxy'.

source.title: Main report para 3.2 (p.1) and para 4.19 (p.5); Appendix B section 8 Minimum Revenue Provision Policy Statement 2026/27 (p.12)

facts.note: The stated intent is 'This will ensure the financial cost aligns with the asset life as per the depreciation method' (para 3.2). Effect quantified in the MRP contribution line of Appendix D B: £5,320k (2024/25 actual) → £5,801k (2025/26, last of old method) → £7,116k (2026/27, +£1,315k / +23%) → £8,997k (2027/28, +£1,881k / +26%) → £9,021k (2028/29). The two big steps are 2026/27 and 2027/28 — the years the new methodology first bites. Net uplift 2025/26 → 2028/29 = +55%.

facts.value: Ratio rises from 4.41% (2024/25 actual) to 7.84% (2028/29 estimate) — nearly doubling. Net Financing Costs £8,453k → £19,993k (+£11,540k). Net Revenue Stream £191,547k → £254,906k (+£63,359k).

facts.note: Steepest single-year jumps: 5.47% → 5.91% (2025/26→2026/27), 5.91% → 7.51% (2026/27→2027/28), 7.51% → 7.84% (2027/28→2028/29). courses_named: Liability Benchmark: using it in practice
officer.body:
Hi Fenella,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep both of those relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts on the Treasury Management Policy and Strategy 2026/27 that went to Finance, Policy and Resources on 12 February and on to Council on 3 March. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The paper is clearly laid out, the MRP methodology change is spelled out more carefully than most, and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Three things worth reading together. Your Appendix D section C shows the ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream rising from 4.41% at 2024/25 actual to 7.84% by 2028/29 estimate — Net Financing Costs go from £8.5m to £20.0m over the five-year window against a Net Revenue Stream growing £63m. Nearly doubling as a ratio, and driven by two forces the paper makes visible one at a time.

The first is your MRP methodology change. Section 3.2 moves you from a 33-year straight-line average to a life-of-asset basis, and Appendix D section B shows what that does numerically: MRP contributions rise from £5.80m in 2025/26 — the last year on the old methodology — to £9.02m by 2028/29, a 55% uplift. The two biggest single-year steps are in 2026/27 (+23%) and 2027/28 (+26%), the years the new methodology first bites. Front-loading MRP against asset life is a substantive policy call and a large part of the ratio rise sits behind that change rather than behind new borrowing itself.

The second is your Appendix D section J interest-rate-risk table, which prints something we don't often see. In 2026/27 a 1% rise helps the revenue account by £186k and a 1% fall hurts it by £349k — the inverse of a fixed-rate borrower's usual position. By 2027/28 the sign flips (+£73k for a rise, -£383k for a fall); by 2028/29 a 1% rise is worth +£577k. A single indicator capturing the pivot from net investor to net borrower as it happens, exactly matching the £145m of new borrowing your paragraph 4.17 anticipates over the next four years and the £45m step Appendix E puts specifically in 2026/27. Your own rider in J — that in 2026/27 the budget assumes external borrowing at year-end, so a rate move has 'the inverse affect compared to future years where there is external borrowing' — is more explanation than most councils give an indicator you can print without.

Behind all this sits the rate forecast on Appendix B page 2, which has 25-year PWLB falling from 5.94% at end-December 2025 to 5.00% by March 2027 — a 94bp fall over 15 months on which the timing of your 2026/27 external draw rests. Live rates at both daily fixings and the market's implied path are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard, so you can see day-by-day where that forecast is holding and where it isn't as you approach the draw window. Every council's PWLB book priced against the DMO's discount curve is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis — one honest flag on our side, our file for Richmond doesn't yet fully reconcile to your December 2025 loan book, a data-quality issue we're working on. We hold PWLB only in any case; the £10.5m MEEF and £5m Barclays sit outside our file by design.

One standing note. CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put the liability benchmark in front of every S151, and your Appendix E — the £45m 2026/27 external borrowing number, honestly caveated as 'only a guide' — is one of the cleaner presentations we've read. Our interactive version at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is fed by live rates so the shape moves as the market does, useful alongside whatever chart MUFG produces.

On training, three of our 115 courses fit what this paper does. MRP: methods and choices covers exactly what your Section 3.2 shift represents. Financing cost ratios and affordability is the companion piece to Appendix D section C. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice sits behind the £45m calculation in Appendix E. All courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.
